title: Banks urge government cuts to curb inflation
full_text:
The chief executives of two of the nation's largest banks have backed cuts in government spending to bring down inflation and make housing more affordable amid warnings the AI building boom could push up the cost of suburban homes as they compete for electricians and plumbers.
Both ANZ boss Nino Matos and his Westpac counterpart Anthony Miller told a parliamentary committee yesterday any cut in government expenditure would help reduce demand and price pressures across an economy that had to become more productive if Australians' living standards were to improve.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers has promised spending cuts in next month's mid-year budget update as the government comes under fire for its management of the economy.
The Reserve Bank last week lifted interest rates for a fifth time this year over concerns that inflation, which has increased to 4.3 per cent, will continue to climb. Central banks around the world are lifting interest rates in part due to the fallout from the war against Iran and the global AI construction boom.
Miller said the inflation problems were fundamentally being driven by the economy's failure to absorb demand stemming from businesses, households and the government.
"Any pull back of demand, public or private, will contribute to reducing the inflationary challenge that we're currently navigating," he said.
Matos noted inflation around the world was being driven by a "super cycle" of spending linked to AI, renewable energy and defence. Cost-of-living pressures were challenging "Western social cohesion", he said, as living standards fell due to higher inflation and higher interest rates. "Any spending reducing in the economy, be it public or private, will take the pressure from inflation. It's just economics," he said.
Figures released by the Australian Bureau of Statistics this week showed the biggest quarterly fall in home loans taken out by investors for existing homes on record with substantial falls as well for the construction of new properties.
Miller said while the government's recent tax changes were aimed at reducing demand, especially from investors, there should be a renewed focus on lifting productivity across housing.
He urged the federal government to consider a "break-glass" plan to let states approve all major infrastructure projects to get projects built faster and more cheaply.
"One area easily in our control is the approval process. It's an anchor on our growth. We will not meet our targets on housing or energy nor will we improve living standards unless we move faster," he said.
After announcing last week's hike in interest rates, Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock said the RBA was not looking to drive the economy into recession.
Matos said the greatest threat to the Australian economy was not a homegrown recession, but one caused by a "blip" in the AI boom.
"We have a very curious situation in the world where we have the equity markets at record highs because of the tech wave and basically because of the AI wave, but at the same time you have record highs of interest rates," he said. "It's a dangerous situation for the world."
The size and speed of the domestic AI construction boom has caught Australian authorities by surprise. Last week the Reserve Bank, which in May had been expecting private sector investment to grow by just 0.8 per cent in 2026, revised up its forecasts to 12 per cent.
Analysis released yesterday by Oxford Economics Australia suggests even that may be conservative. It estimates cumulative spending on data centres could surpass $240 billion by 2030 and be a major driver of the economy. Expenditure climbed from $1 billion in 2020 to $20 billion this year and is forecast to reach $60 billion by the end of the decade.
But that activity will require thousands of extra workers, many already employed in housing construction. Total employment in data centres is expected to peak at 38,400 workers of which 36,000 will be involved in construction. That workforce would include 4500 electricians, about 22 per cent of the total working on major projects right now, and 5600 plumbers.
Oxford economist Oscar Guth said the sharp increase in demand for specialised tradies would increase cost pressures across the entire construction sector.
"The rapid expansion of the data centre pipeline is likely to intensify competition for specialised labour, adding to wage and contractor cost pressures in an environment of already elevated inflation," he said.
On top of the 38,400 jobs connected to data centres, another 84,000 jobs are forecast to be generated through supply chain links to construction with an extra 96,000 created by higher additional spending.
